# Wavelet and Pyramid Transforms

Also called: Transform-based Volume Compression, Multiresolution Wavelet Compression

## Overview
Wavelet and Pyramid Transforms decompose volumetric data into a hierarchy of frequency subbands to enable multi-resolution rendering and high compression ratios [S1][S2, unofficial][S3]. Unlike sibling methods that may use blockwise partitioning [Blockwise Wavelet Compression](6100-blockwise-wavelet-compression.md) or tensor approximations [Tensor-Train Decomposition for 4D Volumes](14070-tensor-train-decomposition-for-4d-volumes.md), this family relies on separable 1D filter banks applied recursively along each axis to create a global multiresolution structure [G].

## Shared principles
See [Value compression](6-value-compression.md) for the shared principles of this family.

## Subtopics

### [Laplacian Pyramid Volume Rendering](2261-laplacian-pyramid-volume-rendering.md)
Laplacian Pyramid Volume Rendering is a direct volume rendering technique that reconstructs voxel values on-the-fly from Laplacian pyramid compressed data, utilizing a cache to minimize redundant reconstruction overhead. It forms a multiresolution representation by pre-applying a Gaussian filter, expansion, and prediction of values, sharing many similarities with wavelet transforms while being optimized for on-the-fly decoding during ray casting.

### [L2 Norm Wavelet Compression](3542-l2-norm-wavelet-compression.md)
L2 Norm Wavelet Compression selects a subset of wavelet coefficients to minimize the $L_2$ error norm of the reconstructed signal relative to the original. It solves the problem of achieving a specific fidelity guarantee while maximizing compression ratio by discarding the smallest magnitude coefficients. It differs from its siblings, such as [Laplacian Pyramid Volume Rendering](2261-laplacian-pyramid-volume-rendering.md) and [Biorthogonal Wavelet Compression](5381-biorthogonal-wavelet-compression.md), by explicitly sorting coefficients by magnitude to enforce a strict global error bound, rather than relying on perceptual models or fixed bit-depth quantization.

### [B-spline Wavelet Compression](5377-b-spline-wavelet-compression.md)
B-spline Wavelet Compression is a method for compressing volumetric data by decomposing it into a hierarchy of scaling and wavelet coefficients using a semi-orthogonal B-spline basis. It solves the problem of efficient storage and transmission of volume data by exploiting the decay of coefficients across scales, specifically addressing the lack of compact support in B-spline dual functions through a matrix-based projection scheme. It sets itself apart from standard orthogonal wavelet transforms by allowing linear complexity construction and smooth basis functions, and from Haar wavelets by providing better approximation properties for smooth data. It builds on [Wavelet and Pyramid Transforms](3856-wavelet-and-pyramid-transforms.md) by implementing the specific B-spline filter bank and matrix operations.

### [Wavelet Slice Compression (Video Coding Approach)](5379-wavelet-slice-compression-video-coding-approach.md)
Wavelet Slice Compression is a volumetric data compression method that partitions a 3D volume into 2D slices and treats them as a sequence of correlated frames, applying video coding techniques to exploit temporal and spatial coherence. This approach separates spatial compression within slices from temporal compression between them, leveraging established video compression principles to achieve higher compression ratios for volumetric data with strong inter-slice correlation.

### [Biorthogonal Wavelet Compression](5381-biorthogonal-wavelet-compression.md)
Biorthogonal Wavelet Compression compresses volumetric data by applying a multilevel wavelet transform and discarding the least significant coefficients to achieve variable compression ratios while preserving reconstruction quality. It partitions the volume into blocks and transforms them independently using biorthogonal filters, such as the 9/7-tap Daubechies wavelet or biorthogonal spline wavelets. Unlike tensor approximation methods which follow a multiscale behavior, this method exhibits multiresolution behavior, making it advantageous for reconstructing the overall statistical distribution of a dataset at coarser resolutions.

### [Wavelet Compression (Haar Basis)](5779-wavelet-compression-haar-basis.md)
Wavelet Compression (Haar Basis) is a lossy or lossless compression method that represents data using a smaller set of coefficients derived from the Haar wavelet basis. It reduces memory footprint and bandwidth by exploiting coefficient sparsity. Unlike sibling methods using biorthogonal filters or packet transforms, this method relies on the orthogonal Haar basis, enabling a globally optimal compression strategy via coefficient thresholding (the "Global Oracle") that minimizes the $L^2$ approximation error for a given number of retained coefficients.

### [Discrete Wavelet Packet Transform](6049-discrete-wavelet-packet-transform.md)
The Discrete Wavelet Packet Transform (DWPT) is a wavelet-based compression method that provides a richer, more flexible decomposition of volume data than the standard Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) by recursively decomposing both approximation and detail coefficients. Unlike standard DWT, which only decomposes the low-frequency approximation subband, DWPT allows for arbitrary tree structures, enabling optimal basis selection for specific data characteristics. It is primarily used in volume segmentation rather than volume rendering.

### [3D Discrete Wavelet Transform](6083-3d-discrete-wavelet-transform.md)
The 3D Discrete Wavelet Transform (3D DWT) is a multiresolution decomposition technique that extends the 2D wavelet algorithm to volumetric data. It solves the problem of efficiently representing 3D scalar fields by decomposing the input volume into approximation and detail subbands, enabling compression and adaptive rendering. Unlike 2D methods, it operates on three-dimensional spatial correlations, and unlike Laplacian pyramids, it uses orthogonal or biorthogonal filter banks that allow for perfect reconstruction without redundancy in the approximation subband.

### [Block-based intra-band prediction](7449-block-based-intra-band-prediction.md)
Block-based intra-band prediction is a lossless compression technique applied to wavelet coefficients to exploit remaining anatomical symmetries and spatial correlations that persist after multi-level decomposition. It operates by predicting a current block of coefficients from previously encoded blocks using geometric transformations (rotations and mirroring), encoding the residual only if it yields a lower bit-rate than encoding the original block. Unlike generic volumetric compression methods, this method is highly specialized for medical images with strong structural symmetries (particularly CT scans) and is ineffective on smooth or non-symmetrical data like MRI or Ultrasound.

### [Lifting-Based Temporal Wavelet Transform](8249-lifting-based-temporal-wavelet-transform.md)
This method computes 1-D temporal wavelet transforms on long image sequences without buffering all slices, thereby avoiding artificial Group of Pictures (GOP) boundaries and the severe quality degradations associated with lossy decoding at those boundaries. It sets itself apart from standard block-based temporal transforms by using a finite buffer to continuously process the sequence, creating the effect of infinite memory through an overlap-save-like mechanism.

### [Independent vectors in every channel](8628-independent-vectors-in-every-channel.md)
A multiresolution compression scheme that extracts $k$-dimensional vectors independently within each channel of the wavelet decomposition hierarchy, without correlating data across different resolution levels. It solves the problem of compressing medical volume data by exploiting spatial redundancy within individual frequency bands while maintaining true multiresolution browsing capabilities, distinguishing it from cross-scale methods that sacrifice resolution adaptability for higher compression ratios.

### [Mask Compression Pipeline](9683-mask-compression-pipeline.md)
The Mask Compression Pipeline is a multi-stage encoding strategy designed to minimize the storage footprint of binarized learnable masks used in neural field representations (such as TensoRF and TriPlane). It solves the problem of high memory consumption caused by storing sparse binary masks by exploiting the statistical properties of these masks (high sparsity, block-wise structure) through 8-bit casting, Run-Length Encoding (RLE), and Huffman coding. It distinguishes itself from general volume compression methods by operating specifically on the *mask* data structure rather than the volumetric coefficients themselves, and by utilizing level-wise separation to handle the varying sparsity patterns across different Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) decomposition levels.

### [Shearlet Transform](10813-shearlet-transform.md)
The Shearlet Transform is a GPU-accelerated implementation of the Alpha Shearlet transform that computes Fourier coefficients once at initialization and performs all subsequent operations on the GPU to allow parallel batch processing. It differs from the AlphaTransforms library by moving all post-initialization operations to the GPU.

### [Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Transform](12543-dual-tree-complex-wavelet-transform.md)
The Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Transform (DTCWT) is a wavelet transform that employs two separate real Discrete Wavelet Transforms (DWTs) to compute the real and imaginary parts of the complex coefficients. Unlike standard real-valued wavelet transforms, DTCWT provides approximate shift invariance and enhanced directional selectivity in 2D and 3D by constructing complex wavelets from pairs of real wavelets. It is distinguished from its siblings, such as [Laplacian Pyramid Volume Rendering](2261-laplacian-pyramid-volume-rendering.md) and [3D Discrete Wavelet Transform](6083-3d-discrete-wavelet-transform.md), by its ability to generate oriented complex subbands that better capture directional features while maintaining near-shift invariance, which is critical for high-fidelity volume data compression and representation.

### [Region of Interest Update Protocol](16206-region-of-interest-update-protocol.md)
Region of Interest Update Protocol is a method for adaptive volume rendering that maintains high resolution in a user-specified sub-volume while keeping the rest of the dataset at a lower resolution, using wavelet transforms to manage the transition. It sets itself apart from global multi-resolution methods by allowing dynamic, localized updates to the high-resolution region without re-transforming the entire dataset, thereby reducing computational overhead during interaction.

### [Piecewise-Linear Haar Transform](17593-piecewise-linear-haar-transform.md)
The Piecewise-Linear Haar (PLHaar) transform is an $n$-bit to $n$-bit wavelet transform used for volume and image compression that operates by applying an octant-dependent rotation in $L_\infty$ space. Unlike the standard Haar transform, PLHaar does not preserve averages, which prevents the "fade to gray" artifact common in thresholded wavelet coding, and it is continuous, making it suitable for both lossless and lossy coding without the discontinuities found in other integer transforms like the S-Transform. It is distinguished from its siblings by its ability to function as an involution using a single lookup table for both forward and inverse operations.

### [Foveated Volume Extraction in Wavelet Domain](20675-foveated-volume-extraction-in-wavelet-domain.md)
Foveated Volume Extraction in Wavelet Domain is a method for extracting a subset of wavelet coefficients required to reconstruct a specific Region of Interest (ROI) at various resolution layers, thereby reducing the data size for transmission and rendering. It solves the problem of efficiently transmitting and rendering high-resolution 3D volume data over networks by focusing computational and bandwidth resources on the user's area of interest. Unlike full-volume reconstruction, this method leverages the hierarchical structure of wavelet transforms to identify and extract only the coefficients necessary to reconstruct the ROI across all resolution layers, achieving significant compression ratios (e.g., a factor of 2,000).

#### Modified Dyadic Wavelet with Rice Coding
- [S1] A method using a modified 3-D dyadic wavelet transform tailored to volumetric medical images and an optimized Rice code of very low complexity for scalable lossless coding.

#### 3D Orthogonal Wavelet Approximation
- [S2, unofficial] A three dimensional wavelet approximation for volume data sets presented by Shigeru Muraki [12].
- [S2, unofficial] Build a 3D orthogonal wavelet basis by using all possible tensor products of one dimensional basis function.
- [S2, unofficial] Apply wavelet transforms to volume data to compute wavelet coefficients.
- [S2, unofficial] Remove insignificant coefficients and only use the remaining coefficients.
- [S2, unofficial] Reconstruct an approximation of the original data from the remaining coefficients.

#### Volumetric Decomposition Structure
- [S3] A labeling notation (x,y,z) representing the number of 1D-DWT decompositions along Horizontal (H), Vertical (V), and Axial (A) dimensions, using the Mallat decomposition structure.
- [S3] Recommended in-slice (XY) decomposition levels: Generally, four levels suffice to efficiently compress images in lossless scenarios.
- [S3] Recommended axial (Z) decomposition levels: Near-optimal efficiency for lossless 5x3 is reached at two levels; for some images, a single decomposition suffices. The bit-rate difference between two levels and the best case is below 0.01 bpp [S3].
- [S3] Performing more decomposition levels than necessary increases processor/memory load and reduces random-access efficiency due to larger support widths.
- [S3] Lossless bit-rate increase relative to (6,6,0) decomposition: Varies by image and number of in-slice decompositions using 5x3 kernel.
- [S3] Lossless bit-rate increase relative to (4,4,4) decomposition: Varies by image and number of axial decompositions using 5x3 kernel.

#### Wavelet Transform on Polygon Meshes
- [S4] Compute the wavelet transform by repeated decomposition, starting with a fine resolution and terminating at the coarse resolution of a base polygon.
- [S4] For a regular, rectilinear mesh, apply the corresponding one-dimensional operation to the rows and columns.
- [S4] To optimize, change the order of computation in an s-lift operation so that every vertex is modified only once, rather than updating vertices v twice.
- [S4] Store the coordinates of the base vertices, the connectivity of the base mesh, and the wavelet coefficients. Quantize the wavelet coefficients and compress them using arithmetic coding.
- [S4] Wavelet coefficients have two coordinates, representing points and vectors in the plane.
- [S4] For mesh boundaries, all boundary vertices must be transformed by the one-dimensional lifting operations (equations 3.2 and 3.3) to ensure correct transformation.
- [S4] The operations are well-defined for extraordinary vertices (vertices that do not have four incident edges) and for arbitrary polygons in a base mesh.

## Background
The use of wavelets for volume rendering and compression emerged in the late 1990s and early 2000s as a solution to the memory bandwidth bottleneck in GPU-based direct volume rendering (DVR) [G]. Early work by Guthe et al. [S2, unofficial] demonstrated hierarchical wavelet representations allowing compression ratios of 30:1 without noticeable artifacts. The Laplacian pyramid approach [GY95] described in [S1] uses low-pass filtering and delta computation for on-the-fly reconstruction. Wetekam et al. [WSKW05] proposed an octree-based multiresolution approach with FPGA hardware decoding [S1]. Wu et al. [WQ05] introduced a modified 3-D dyadic wavelet transform with Rice coding for medical images [S1]. Shigeru Muraki [S2, unofficial] presented 3D orthogonal wavelet approximations using tensor products. The field continues to evolve with neural field representations requiring specialized mask compression [S1][S2, unofficial].
